Write an email to a colleague about how the falling cost of making things might change why people work. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: How cheaper making might change why we work

Hi Sam,

I've been thinking about something since our conversation last week, and I wanted to get it down while it's fresh.

The cost of making things is falling fast. Three-dimensional printing, open-source hardware, cheap cloud tools, and now AI that can write code and draw up designs in minutes: all of these let one person do what once took a team and a budget. A decade ago, if you wanted to build a product, you needed capital, a factory, and a lot of people. Today you need a laptop and a good idea (and maybe a few evenings).

So what happens to work when the barrier to making drops this low?

My guess is that the reason people work will shift. For a long time, most of us worked because we needed access to the machinery: the factory, the office, the large organization that owned the tools. The job was the price of admission. When the tools are nearly free, that price goes away. People will still work, of course, but they will choose where to spend their effort based on different things: purpose, mastery, and the people they get to work with.

I see this already in open source communities. Nobody pays most contributors to show up. They show up because they feel appreciated, because the problem is interesting, and because they're getting better at something they care about. In other words, the energy comes from the work and the environment rather than from the paycheck alone.

If that spreads, organizations will have to compete on something other than control of resources. They'll need to offer a place where people feel valued and motivated. That's a big change from the Industrial-era model of interchangeable skills and tight hierarchy, and it favors more specialized, artisan-style mastery.

There is a catch, though. Cheap making also means cheap competition. If anyone can build the thing, then what you build matters less than why and how you build it. Trust, taste, and community become the scarce resources.

I'd love to hear whether you think I'm overstating this, especially from your experience on the hardware side. Could we grab thirty minutes this week to talk it through? I'm also happy to sketch the idea in a simple diagram first if that would help.

Thanks,
